beats.say: Good news from the coast: the world's mangrove forests are growing back.
A new study, shared by NASA, read forty years of Landsat satellite images, from 1984 to 2023.
From 1984 to 2010, the world lost nearly three thousand square kilometres of mangroves.
Then, around 2010, the trend flipped. Since then, mangroves have gained nearly two thousand.
Satellites can see them because living leaves reflect lots of near-infrared light, so forest stands out from mud and water.
About two thirds of the gain is brand new ground, where mangroves spread onto fresh land.
Rivers carry mud to the sea. It settles into new mudflats, and mangrove seedlings take root there.
The other third is regrowth, where damaged forests recovered or were restored.
And mangroves can store up to four times more carbon than inland tropical forests.
